opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because I think there's a common reaction when people first hear about singular learning theory. They say, "Okay, sure, neural networks have these symmetries. If you've got a ReLU network, you can scale the incoming weights to a neuron up by some constant and the outgoing weights down by the same constant, and the function doesn't change. Or you can permute the hidden neurons. But those are kind of boring. They're just bookkeeping. Why should anyone care?"

I'd make two points about that.

The first is that those generic symmetries really are, in a sense, the least interesting part of the story. If all the degeneracy in neural networks came from scaling and permutation symmetries, you could quotient them out, and you'd be left with something that looks fairly regular. Classical statistical learning theory would apply more or less unchanged. So in that narrow sense, the skeptics are right: the trivial symmetries alone don't justify a whole new theory.

The second point is the important one. The degeneracies that matter in singular learning theory aren't these global symmetries that hold everywhere in parameter space. They're the ones that depend on where you are, on the particular parameter, the data distribution, and the structure the network has actually learned. Take a neuron that's dead on the data distribution. Its incoming weights are then completely unconstrained, and that's a large degenerate direction. But it only exists because of how that neuron relates to the data. Or take two neurons computing nearly the same thing, so that you can trade weight between them. Or a circuit whose downstream reader ignores some of its outputs. These are data-dependent, local degeneracies, and they're intimately tied to the computational structure of the solution.

What the theory says is that the geometry of the set of good solutions, and in particular how degenerate it is as measured by the local learning coefficient, controls things like generalization and which solutions the learning process prefers. Solutions with more degeneracy, meaning lower effective dimension, occupy more volume in a precise sense, so Bayesian learning, and plausibly SGD to a significant extent, is drawn toward them. So degeneracy isn't just a nuisance in the parametrization. It's a measure of how simple the learned algorithm is, in a way that's sensitive to internal structure and not just to the input-output function.

So my answer is this. The trivial symmetries are a nice entry point, a toy example showing that the map from parameters to functions isn't one-to-one. But you shouldn't stop there and conclude that degeneracy is trivial. The deeper claim is that the non-generic degeneracies, the ones that emerge from learning, carry real information about what the network has learned and how it's organized internally. That's exactly the information we'd want for interpretability and alignment, and it's why we've put so much effort into estimating the local learning coefficient in real models and tracking how it changes during training. When it jumps or drops, that often lines up with the network forming or reorganizing some internal structure, a developmental stage if you like.

So I'd turn the question around. The trivial symmetries are where intuition starts. The degeneracies that aren't trivial are where the science is.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I get a lot, and I think it's worth being careful about, because there's a cheap answer and a more interesting answer.

The cheap answer is that scaling symmetries are, in some sense, boring. If you have a ReLU network, you can multiply the incoming weights to a neuron by some positive constant and divide the outgoing weights by the same constant, and the function the network computes doesn't change. So you get these continuous families of parameters that all represent the same thing. That's a degeneracy in the sense that the Fisher information matrix, the Hessian of the loss, is going to have zero eigenvalues along those directions. And people sometimes look at singular learning theory and say, well, this is all it's about, it's just counting these trivial symmetries, and that can't be very interesting because they're the same everywhere in parameter space.

And that last part is roughly right. If a degeneracy is present uniformly, at every point, then it doesn't help you distinguish one solution from another. The whole point of the learning coefficient, the local learning coefficient, is that it varies across parameter space, and that variation is what carries information about the structure of what's been learned. A symmetry that's there no matter what you've learned just shifts everything by a constant. So from the perspective of model selection, or of understanding why a network ends up in one basin rather than another, the scaling symmetries alone are not where the action is.

But I'd push back on the word trivial, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that the interesting degeneracies and the trivial ones are not cleanly separable. The scaling symmetry is a generic feature, but when you also have, say, a dead neuron, or two neurons whose weights have become aligned so they're computing the same feature, or some part of the network whose output is being multiplied by something close to zero downstream, then those extra degeneracies interact with the scaling ones. The geometry of the level sets of the loss near a point is a single object. You can't really take the scaling part out and look at the remainder in isolation; the way these things compound is exactly what determines the local learning coefficient. So the "trivial" symmetries are part of the ambient structure in which the non-trivial stuff lives, and the counting only makes sense once you take all of it together.

The second reason is historical, or maybe sociological. The scaling symmetries are the thing that first makes it undeniable that neural networks are singular models. Before you get into the subtle stuff, someone can just show you with two lines of algebra that the parameter-to-function map is not injective, and that the Fisher information is degenerate, and therefore the whole regular statistics toolkit, the Laplace approximation, BIC, asymptotic normality of the posterior, all of that is simply not valid for these models. Watanabe's theory exists because of that fact. So I'd say the scaling symmetries are trivial in the sense that they're easy to see, but they're significant in the sense that they're the clearest demonstration that you need a different theory.

And then there's a third thing, which I think is actually the most interesting. People sometimes assume that because a symmetry is "just a reparametrization", it has no effect on learning dynamics. But stochastic gradient descent doesn't see functions, it sees parameters. The flat directions created by scaling symmetries are directions along which the loss is constant but the noise in SGD still moves you. And there's work, going back to things like the Dinh et al. observations about sharpness, and more recently on how the effective learning rate interacts with weight norm, showing that where you are along a scaling orbit does affect how training proceeds, even though it doesn't affect what the network currently computes. So the symmetry is trivial for the function but not trivial for the process that finds the function.

So my overall assessment is something like: scaling symmetries by themselves are not what singular learning theory is trying to measure, and if that were all there was we'd have a rather dull theory. But they're the entry point, they're not separable from the degeneracies we do care about, and they have real consequences for dynamics. I'd resist the instinct to wave them away. What I'd want to resist even more is the opposite error, which is to think that once you've found a few obvious symmetries you've understood the geometry. The actual geometry near the solutions that SGD finds is far richer than that, and most of it has nothing to do with a symmetry group at all.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s tempting to dismiss them as a kind of bookkeeping issue. If you can multiply the weights in one layer by a constant and compensate in the next layer, leaving the function unchanged, you might say, well, we’ve just described the same thing in multiple ways. Why should that matter?

But it matters because we train in parameter space, while what we care about is the function the network computes. The relationship between those two spaces is not one-to-one. So a picture in which every good solution is an isolated point, with a nice quadratic loss around it, is already missing something.

Now, a simple scaling symmetry may be something you can account for by choosing a different parameterization. I wouldn’t claim that this symmetry alone explains the interesting behavior of neural networks. The more substantial issue is that there are many ways for parameters to become redundant, and those redundancies can change depending on where you are in parameter space. A hidden unit becoming inactive, for example, can make other parameters irrelevant.

So I see these seemingly trivial examples as an entry point. They make it concrete that the geometry can be singular. The question then is which aspects of that geometry actually influence learning and generalization, and which are merely artifacts of how we’ve chosen to describe the model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s easy to dismiss them as bookkeeping: you can rescale one layer and compensate in the next, so many different parameter values describe exactly the same function. Why not just identify those points and move on?

But that intuition comes from thinking of the space of functions as something smooth and well behaved. The symmetry can interact with other degeneracies—for example, when a weight or an entire neuron becomes zero—and then the geometry is much more interesting. Identifying equivalent parameters doesn’t automatically give you a nice, regular space.

From the perspective of singular learning theory, the important question is how much volume in parameter space corresponds to functions that are nearly optimal. That influences Bayesian inference and the complexity of the model in a way that simply counting parameters doesn’t capture.

So I wouldn’t say every scaling symmetry is, by itself, some profound explanation of deep learning. But I also wouldn’t throw it away as trivial. It’s an accessible example of why the geometry underlying these models differs from the geometry assumed in classical statistics.
